LESSON 25 OF 106·Network Attacks and Defences

Secure Remote Access in Practice

What remote access exposes and how to build it properly: strong authentication, device checks, narrow privileges and session evidence — from VPN to per-application access.

Foundation13 min
Why this matters

Remote access concentrates a difficult problem: granting a user on an untrusted network the same reach as a user in an office. The design question is what the connection grants, and for how long.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A remote access system authenticates the user and the device, then decides what the session is allowed to reach.
  • Publishing the whole internal network to a remote client gives away far more than most users need.
  • Publishing individual applications narrows that, and per-request authorisation narrows it further.
  • Long-lived credentials on a shared device mean the access outlives the person who asked for it.
  • Session recording and per-request logs are what make remote access auditable after the fact.

The background

  • Remote access began as a dial-up modem and a protocol that gave full network access, which is why it was trusted implicitly.
  • VPN clients moved that model to the internet without changing its shape, so full network access became the default expectation.
  • Application-level access grew as organisations became uncomfortable exposing entire internal ranges.
  • Zero-trust access management moved the decision from network location to identity and device posture on each request.

Real-world examples

  • A VPN account that still works after someone leaves is one of the most common and most damaging findings in an assessment.
  • Split tunnelling on a lost laptop can leave corporate traffic unprotected while the device is on hostile Wi-Fi.
  • An access system that trusts the internal network implicitly is only as strong as every device on that network.

What to look for

  • List every remote access account and check whether it still belongs to someone who needs it.
  • Check what each account can reach, and whether that matches the person actual job.
  • Look for shared remote credentials, and for accounts that bypass multi-factor authentication.
  • Confirm that sessions are logged well enough to answer who accessed what, and when.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

NIST SP 800-46 Rev. 2 — remote access guidance

Reading the official guidance on enterprise telework and remote-access security, then checking your own remote paths against its recommendations

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Grant access to the applications a person needs rather than to the whole network.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for remote access and for every administrative path.
  • Remove access automatically when someone leaves or changes role, rather than on a schedule.
  • Re-authenticate periodically during long sessions so a stolen connection has a limited useful life.
  • Combine remote access with device health checks, so unmanaged devices do not receive the same access as managed ones.
